title: Research Methods for the Social Sciences
summary: Learn to design and carry out social research: research questions and variables, quantitative methods and sample sizes, qualitative interviews and thematic analysis, mixed methods and secondary data, analysis and presentation, and ethics and writing up.
audience: University students, postgraduate researchers, NGO and government researchers

body.p: Social research systematically collects and analyses evidence to answer questions about people and society. Good research starts with a clear, focused question, not with a method.

list: Topic: youth unemployment.
Narrower focus: graduates in one city.
Research question: "What factors are associated with how long graduates in Kisumu take to find their first job?"
Hypothesis (for quantitative work): "Graduates who completed internships find jobs faster than those who did not."
Variables: characteristics that vary, such as age, income or job status. The independent variable is the presumed cause; the dependent variable is the outcome.
Operationalisation: defining how you will measure a concept, such as "employment" as having paid work for at least 10 hours a week.
Unit of analysis: individuals, households, schools or countries.
Research designs: cross-sectional (one point in time), longitudinal (over time), experimental (with random assignment) and case study (in-depth study of one or a few cases).

body.tip: Write your research question as a single sentence and test whether it could actually be answered with evidence you can collect.

body.p: Quantitative research measures variables numerically to describe patterns and test relationships, often through surveys, experiments and secondary data such as censuses.

list: Population: everyone you want to draw conclusions about.
Probability sampling (simple random, stratified, cluster) allows generalisation with known margins of error.
Non-probability sampling (convenience, purposive, snowball) is easier but limits generalisation.

body.p: For estimating a proportion with 95% confidence, a common formula is n = 1.96² x p(1 - p) / E², using p = 0.5 when unsure. For a margin of error E of 5%, n = 3.8416 x 0.25 / 0.0025, about 384.2, so 385 respondents; for 3%, about 1068. If you expect a 70% response rate, you must invite 385 / 0.7, about 550 people.

list: Use clear, simple, neutral wording; avoid leading or double-barrelled questions ("Is the service fast and friendly?").
Offer complete, non-overlapping answer options.
Pilot the questionnaire with a few people first.
Translate carefully and back-translate to check meaning.

body.tip: Decide how you will analyse each question before you ask it; if you cannot, the question may not be needed.

body.p: Qualitative research explores meanings, experiences and processes in depth, using words, observations and images rather than numbers.

list: In-depth interviews: semi-structured conversations guided by a topic list, allowing follow-up questions.
Focus groups: guided discussions with about 6 to 10 participants, useful for exploring shared views and language.
Participant observation: watching and taking part in settings.
Document and media analysis: policies, newspapers, social-media posts.
Purposive sampling: choosing participants who can best inform the question; interviews often continue until little new emerges (saturation).

steps: Read and re-read to become familiar with the data.
Code: label meaningful segments of text.
Review themes against the data and look for exceptions.
Write up with illustrative quotations and interpretation.

body.p: Quality in qualitative research is judged by credibility, transparency, reflexivity about the researcher's influence and how well conclusions are grounded in data.

body.tip: Keep a memo diary of emerging ideas during analysis; insights fade if not written down.

lessons.title: Mixed methods, case studies and secondary data

body.p: Mixed-methods research combines quantitative and qualitative approaches to give a fuller picture. A survey might show that 60% of households (72 of 120) have reduced meals in the past month; follow-up interviews explain why and how families cope.

list: Explanatory sequential: survey first, then interviews to explain results.
Exploratory sequential: interviews first, then a survey to test how widespread the findings are.
Convergent: both at the same time, compared at the end.
Case studies: in-depth study of a school, organisation, programme or community using multiple sources.

body.p: Existing data, such as censuses, demographic and health surveys, labour force surveys, administrative records and Afrobarometer, can answer many questions cheaply. Check how the data were collected, definitions, coverage and dates before using them.

body.tip: Search for existing datasets before collecting new data; it may save months of fieldwork.

body.p: Start with descriptive statistics: counts, percentages, means and medians, and charts. Then look at relationships between variables.

A cross-tabulation shows how one variable varies with another. If 45 of 80 graduates who did internships found work within six months (56.25%), compared with a lower share among those without internships, there is an association worth testing. Always report percentages within the right group and give the base numbers.

list: Response rate: completed responses divided by people invited.
Statistical tests (such as chi-square or t-tests) check whether differences are larger than chance would explain.
Correlation and regression examine relationships between numerical variables.
Association is not causation: confounding variables such as family income may explain both internships and job success.

body.p: Use clear tables and charts with titles, labels and sources. In a sample of 400, a 25% figure represents 100 people; showing both helps readers judge results.

body.tip: Write results first in plain sentences, then add statistics to support them.

body.p: Research involving people must protect them from harm and respect their rights.

list: Informed consent: participants understand the purpose, risks and their right to refuse or withdraw.
Confidentiality and anonymity: protect identities, especially on sensitive topics.
Do no harm: consider emotional, social, legal and physical risks; have referral information ready for distressed participants.
Special care with children and vulnerable groups, often requiring parental consent and extra safeguards.
Ethics approval: universities and many institutions require approval from a research ethics committee before data collection.
Data protection: store data securely and follow laws such as POPIA and the Nigeria Data Protection Act.

body.p: A research report usually includes an abstract, introduction and research question, literature review, methodology, findings, discussion, limitations, conclusion and references. Be honest about limitations, reference sources accurately in the required style, and share findings with participants and communities where possible.

body.tip: Describe your methods clearly enough that another researcher could repeat your study.
